issues.description: The problem statement and UML specify a StockIngredient constructor with signature StockIngredient(String, int, int), but the template StockIngredient class only provides a constructor with signature StockIngredient(String, int, int, boolean). This prevents students from instantiating StockIngredient using the three-argument constructor as expected (e.g., new StockIngredient(name, price, quantity)), causing compilation failures when implementing SealSaloon.acceptSupplyDelivery or following examples in the problem/template.
issues.suggestedFix: Add or restore a three-parameter constructor StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity) in the template StockIngredient class (e.g., as an overload that delegates to the existing constructor or implements the intended validation). This will align the template with the problem specification and the solution, allowing students to create StockIngredient instances with three arguments.

issues.description: The problem statement UML and the reference solution expect a StockIngredient constructor with signature StockIngredient(String, int, int), but the template repository defines only StockIngredient(String, int, int, boolean). This mismatch forces students to deal with an unexpected constructor signature (or to add an overload) when implementing SealSaloon and when creating StockIngredient instances, causing compilation errors and unnecessary cognitive overhead.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the template with the problem and solution by providing a StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity) constructor. For minimal change, add an overloaded 3-argument constructor that delegates to the existing 4-argument one (e.g., public StockIngredient(String name, int price, int quantity) { this(name, price, quantity, true); }).
